summary:
ILoveMars (ARES NAV // Martian Survival) is an interactive 3D planetary navigation and mission-planning platform built for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Powered by CesiumJS, the web application integrates multi-spectral NASA datasets—Optical (Viking MDIM 2.1 & MRO CTX), Elevation (MGS MOLA), Thermal (MGS TES), Radiation (MSL RAD), and Hydrated Minerals (Mars Odyssey GRS H₂O)—alongside 152 searchable landmarks, active spacecraft tracking, and dual Earth UTC / Mars Coordinated Time (MTC) clocks.
Because Mars lacks GPS, a global magnetic field, and breathable air, explorers face severe navigation, radiation, and resource risks. ILoveMars directly solves this with two analytical engines:
• Optimal Survival Routing: Calculates radiation-safe, thermally viable paths between two coordinates while prioritizing rover encounters and Orbiter Relay Corridors.
• Site Habitability Analysis: Scores user-selected regions (0–100) by weighting Water/ISRU availability (30%), Radiation (25%), Thermal stability (25%), and Terrain/Atmosphere (20%).
By transforming complex NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) archives into an actionable survival cockpit, ILoveMars empowers future astronauts to plan safe Marswalks and select viable base sites.
details:
Project Details — ILoveMars (https://ilovemars.ai.studio)

What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

ILoveMars is a browser-based 3D planetary navigation and mission-planning cockpit built for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Using CesiumJS, the platform renders a high-resolution, interactive 3D Martian globe backed by real Hipparcos/Tycho-2 astronomical starfield data and dual Earth UTC / Mars Coordinated Time (MTC) mission clocks.

Explorers can switch between multi-spectral planetary layers and run real-time mission-planning simulations:

  • Multi-Layer Planetary Visualization: Integrates Optical imagery (Viking Orbiter MDIM 2.1 at 232 m/px & MRO CTX at 6 m/px), Elevation (MGS MOLA at 463 m/px), Thermal (MGS TES composite), Radiation (MSL RAD surface dosimetry), Hydrated Minerals (Mars Odyssey GRS H₂O), and Atmospheric Weather overlays across 152 searchable Martian landmarks and active rover/orbiter tracks.
  • Optimal Survival Routing: Computes multi-criteria paths between any two Martian coordinates, evaluating path distance trade-offs, mean and peak radiation exposure (mSv/day), surface temperature windows, MOLA terrain elevation, rover encounter proximity, and Satellite Relay Overflight Corridors (including Mangalyaan, Polar NavSat, and Nozomi).
  • Site Habitability Analysis: Allows users to draw a custom bounding box anywhere on Mars to calculate a weighted habitability score (0–100) across Water/ISRU availability (30%), Radiation safety (25%), Thermal stability (25%), and Terrain & Atmospheric conditions (20%).
  • Surface RDF Beacon & Rover Relay Simulation: Models 400 MHz VHF/UHF radio propagation using free-space path loss and MOLA knife-edge ridge diffraction to solve surface communications where GPS and a global magnetic field do not exist.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Raw planetary science datasets from NASA's Planetary Data System (PDS) are typically scattered across specialized archives and complex GIS formats. ILoveMars unifies these datasets into an intuitive, zero-login web application accessible on both desktop and mobile browsers.

  • For Future Astronauts & Mission Planners: Demonstrates how multi-dataset fusion turns static orbital maps into real-time survival intelligence for planning safe Marswalks, maintaining line-of-sight communications, and scouting In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) base sites.
  • For Students, Educators & Researchers: Makes authentic Martian topography, radiation environments, and mission telemetry engaging and immediately understandable for anyone exploring the Red Planet.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered

  • Solving Mars-Specific Navigation Constraints: Because Mars lacks GPS satellites and a protective magnetosphere, our team prioritized non-GPS navigation (Surface RDF Beacons + orbiter overflight windows) and cumulative radiation/thermal hazard avoidance rather than simple shortest-distance routing.
  • Scientific Integrity & Scale Transparency: Our team accounted for dataset caveats—such as orbital archive temporal coverage vs. live weather, approximate USGS feature footprints, and intentional ~1,000x visual scale enlargement of spacecraft sprites so orbiters and rovers remain clearly visible from orbital altitude.
  • Smooth Cross-Device Performance: Implemented delta-time (dt) normalized camera inertia and altitude-scoped atmospheric rendering so the 3D globe glides smoothly across varying screen refresh rates and devices.

Tools, Coding Languages, Data Sources & Software Used

  • Frontend & 3D Geospatial Engine: TypeScript, React, HTML5/CSS3, Tailwind CSS, Vite, and CesiumJS (3D planetary rendering, camera physics, and spatial overlays).
    • Optical & Topographic: NASA/USGS Viking Orbiter MDIM 2.1 (232 m/px), NASA/Caltech MRO CTX (6 m/px), and NASA/GSFC MGS MOLA (463 m/px).
    • Thermal, Radiation & Water: NASA PDS MGS TES (DOI: 10.17189/xhqz-zw13), MSL Curiosity RAD dosimetry, Mars Odyssey GRS H₂O abundance, and NASA SWIM subsurface water-ice mapping.
    • Spacecraft & Background Provenance: Telemetry and imagery credits to NASA/JPL-Caltech, MSSS, ESA, CNSA, ISRO ISSDC, Wikimedia Commons, and Hipparcos/Tycho-2 astronomical star catalogs (NASA/Goddard SVS / CesiumJS).
  • AI Assistance & Tool Disclosure: In accordance with NASA Space Apps guidelines, our team utilized Google AI Studio / Gemini, Manus, and OpenHands during development for code architecture, CesiumJS geospatial debugging, dataset structuring, UI refinement, and generating custom SVG/vector spacecraft sprites. All scientific modeling logic, data integration, and final verification were directed and reviewed by our team
